findings.claim: Tear resistance is highest parallel to the grain direction.
findings.truth: Tear resistance is lowest along the grain. A tear runs straight and easily in the grain (machine) direction because it follows the fibres; tearing across the grain has to break fibres and needs more force. The lesson's own flashcard and glossary already say paper 'tears more cleanly along' the grain, so the sentence also contradicted the rest of the lesson.
findings.evidence: Standard papermaking property (Elmendorf tear is higher in the cross direction); internal contradiction with lesson 1 flashcard 10 and the 'machine direction' glossary entry.

findings.claim: paper is considerably stiffer when bent against the grain
findings.truth: Paper is stiffer along the grain (the machine direction), where the fibres lie. The Key Fact box in the same lesson says 'stiffer along the grain' and knowledge check 4 marks 'along' as the correct answer, so the body text marked the keyed answer wrong.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Paper machine (fibre orientation gives higher stiffness in the machine direction); internal contradiction with lesson 1 Key Fact and knowledge_checks[3].correct.

findings.claim: Cartridge paper - a thick, slightly textured paper (90-135 g/m2)
findings.truth: Cartridge paper is normally taught and sold at 120-150 g/m2. 90 g/m2 is copier/layout weight, so a student quoting the lower figure could be marked wrong on a 'state a typical weight' question.
findings.evidence: Standard GCSE D&T material tables; spec 8 requires grammage in gsm.

findings.claim: [3].marks: 'Paper and board are considerably stiffer when bent against the grain, so aligning the grain along the fold lines reduces the force needed to score and crease.'
findings.truth: The mark scheme repeated the reversed claim in F2. The accurate point is that board is harder to fold across the grain, which is why fold lines are set parallel to the grain.
findings.evidence: Same as F2; internal consistency with the corrected body text.

findings.claim: a simple rule of thumb is that 1 micron ~ 1 g/m2 for uncoated boards
findings.truth: Uncoated board has a density of roughly 0.7 g/cm3, so 1 g/m2 is about 1.4 microns of thickness. The lesson's own figures prove it: 280-350 g/m2 boxboard is quoted at 400-500 microns, a ratio of about 1.4, not 1.
findings.evidence: Recomputation from the lesson's own cereal-box figures (400/280 = 1.43; 500/350 = 1.43).

findings.claim: The duplex board bullet contains the sentence 'Used for food packaging, cereal boxes and cosmetics cartons where a high-quality printed surface is required at moderate cost.' twice in a row.
findings.truth: Duplicated text; the second copy is deleted.

findings.claim: This is the international standard used across all Eduqas specification and design work.
findings.truth: House rule: an Eduqas/WJEC lesson must never name the board in student-facing prose. Replaced with neutral wording.

findings.claim: bonding two or more plies of material together increases bending stiffness far more than adding the same total thickness as a single ply (repeated in flashcard 5)
findings.truth: A well-bonded laminate is at best as stiff as a solid sheet of the same total thickness, not stiffer. The real gain is that laminating builds up thickness, and bending stiffness rises with roughly the cube of thickness, so doubling thickness makes a board about eight times stiffer.
findings.evidence: Beam theory (second moment of area proportional to t^3); spec in-depth item 3 (stiffening by laminating and cross-section design).

findings.claim: uncoated cartridge (80-120 g/m2) for books and letterheads
findings.truth: Cartridge is a drawing paper, not a book or letterhead stock, and 80-120 g/m2 sits below its normal 120-150 g/m2 band. Books and letterheads use uncoated bond or offset paper at 80-120 g/m2.
findings.evidence: Standard paper trade grades; conflicts with lesson 1 of this unit and with the sibling unit materials-and-properties.

findings.truth: Imposition is a pre-press operation, not a finishing one. The spec lists it under 'Pre-press operations: Grids, registration marks, layout, imposition and colour separation'.

findings.claim: [2] 'Kiss cutting ... stops short of the _____ paper' keys 'backing' as correct while offering 'liner' as a distractor.
findings.truth: 'Liner' (release liner) is the standard trade term for label backing paper, so a well-informed student picking it would be marked wrong. The distractor is replaced with 'laminate'.
findings.evidence: Self-adhesive label construction (face stock / adhesive / release liner).

findings.claim: Flexography is the dominant process for printing on corrugated board, plastic carrier bags, food wrappers and newspaper supplements.
findings.truth: Newspapers and their supplements are printed by web offset (coldset) or gravure in the UK, not flexography. Flexo's dominant markets are corrugated board, flexible film, paper sacks and self-adhesive labels.
findings.evidence: Commercial print practice; spec in-depth item 5 (on-press operations).

findings.claim: when sent to landfill or composted, they break down naturally within months rather than centuries (repeated in flashcard 5 and the 8-mark mark scheme)
findings.truth: Paper breaks down in months in compost or soil, but buried landfill waste has almost no oxygen and paper degrades very slowly there. Stated as written, it teaches a settled misconception.
findings.evidence: Anaerobic landfill decomposition is well documented (landfill excavation studies routinely recover legible decades-old newsprint).

findings.claim: Major technology brands have announced commitments to replace all plastic packaging with moulded pulp alternatives by the end of this decade.
findings.truth: No source supports an industry-wide pledge to replace all plastic packaging with moulded pulp by 2030. Individual firms have committed to removing plastic from packaging. Softened to what is documented.
findings.evidence: No verifiable source found; WebSearch budget exhausted, so the claim is reduced rather than restated with a figure.

findings.claim: Grain direction - orienting the board so the machine direction (grain) runs parallel to the longest fold lines maximises stiffness in the direction where the packaging must resist bending under load.
findings.truth: The stated reason is the wrong one. Fold lines are set parallel to the grain because the board creases cleanly that way and does not crack; stiffness of the finished panels is a secondary effect.
findings.evidence: Lesson 2 flashcard 6 and lesson 3 flashcard 12 both give the correct reason.

findings.claim: a typical carton-board die-cutter can process tens of thousands of sheets per hour (repeated in practice_questions[3].marks)
findings.truth: Flatbed carton die-cutters run at roughly 7,000-11,000 sheets per hour; 'tens of thousands' applies only to rotary corrugated lines. Not corrected because no source could be verified within the WebSearch budget and no mark turns on the figure.
findings.evidence: Manufacturer throughput figures could not be verified in-session.

findings.claim: imposition: 'The arrangement of nets or printed pages on a sheet to minimise material waste during cutting.'
findings.truth: The packaging sense given is defensible, but the definition omits the sense most mark schemes want: arranging pages on the press sheet so they fall in the right order and position after folding and trimming. Left as is because the packaging usage is genuine.
findings.evidence: spec in-depth item 5 lists imposition among pre-press operations alongside layout and colour separation.

findings.claim: Below 170 g/m2 is generally classed as paper; above 170 g/m2 is classed as card or board.
findings.truth: Within the accepted 170-220 gsm band and left alone, but the sibling unit design-technology-eduqas / materials-and-properties teaches 'generally above 200 gsm' and cartridge at 100-140 gsm. The subject should settle on one set of figures across units.
findings.ruling: NOTE: keep 170 gsm and cartridge 120-150 gsm here; sibling materials-and-properties (200 gsm / 100-140) to be re-stamped to match in its own pass - recorded in corpus_notes

summary: Five lessons checked against the Eduqas C600QS in-depth papers and boards content; 18 findings, 14 fixed with 17 edits. The serious ones are a reversed grain-direction pair in lesson 1 (tear resistance and stiffness) that contradicted the lesson's own Key Fact and knowledge-check key, and a house-rule breach in lesson 2 that names the exam board in student-facing prose. Exam claims, mark totals and question forms all match the spec: 2-hour written paper, 100 marks, untiered, no SPaG, no fabricated examiner wording found.
